blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an array `nums`, rearrange its values **in place** so that it becomes a valid **min-heap** — every parent `nums[i]` is less than or equal to its children `nums[2i + 1]` and `nums[2i + 2]` — and return it. Any valid heap is accepted.

blocks.alt: The array 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2 drawn as a tree is not a heap: 9 sits on top of smaller values. After building a heap the same values read 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7: every parent is smaller than or equal to its children, with 1 on top.

blocks.code:
nums = [9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2]   ->  [1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7]   (other valid heaps are fine too)
nums = [3, 2, 1]            ->  [1, 2, 3]
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]         ->  [1, 2, 3, 4]         (already a heap: nothing moves)

blocks.text: Fun fact: a **sorted** array is always a valid min-heap — every parent sits at a smaller index than its children. So sorting solves this in O(n log n). The question is whether we can do better.
1. Brute force: push every value into a new heap
The straightforward way: start an empty heap and push the values one by one. Each push adds at the end and sifts up, so the new array is a heap at every step.
**Time O(n log n), space O(n)** for the second array.
We don't need a second array. Treat the front of `nums` as a growing heap: `nums[0..end-1]` is already a heap, and `nums[end]` joins it by sifting up — exactly a push, without copying anything.

blocks.alt: The array 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2 split into a heap at the front and values still waiting behind it. The next value joins the heap at the boundary and sifts up.

elements.text: after 9, 4 and 7: the front three already form a heap; 1 sifts up next
elements.originalText: after 9, 4 and 7: the front three already form a heap; 1 sifts up next

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space O(1).** Still n sift-ups, and the values that join last — half of all of them — sit on the bottom level and may have to climb the whole height of the tree.
The key idea: sift down, from the bottom up

Flip it around. Every **leaf** is already a heap of one — and half the nodes are leaves. So start at the **last parent**, index `⌊n/2⌋ − 1`, and walk back to the root, sifting each parent **down**. When you reach index `i`, both of its subtrees are already heaps, so one sift down makes the subtree at `i` a heap too.

blocks.alt: Building a heap from 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2 bottom up. Start: indexes 3, 4 and 5 are leaves, already heaps. Index 2: 7 is bigger than its child 2, so they swap. Index 1: 4 is bigger than its child 1, so they swap. Index 0: 9 sinks two levels, swapping with 1 and then with 4. The result is 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7.
blocks.caption: Green subtrees are already heaps. Each sift down joins two of them under one more parent.

blocks.text: A value only sinks as far as the bottom of the tree, and **most nodes are already near the bottom**. In a heap of n values, about n/2 are leaves and don't move at all; n/4 can sink at most 1 level; n/8 at most 2; and only the root can sink the full height.

blocks.alt: A complete tree of 15 nodes, each labelled with how many levels it can sink at most: the 8 leaves 0, the 4 nodes above them 1, the 2 above those 2, and the root 3. The total is 4 plus 4 plus 3, which is 11 — less than the 15 nodes.
blocks.caption: Each node shows the most levels it could sink.

blocks.text: Add it up: n/4 · 1 + n/8 · 2 + n/16 · 3 + … — that sum stays **below n**, however big n gets. Pushing one by one is the opposite: the values that arrive last sit at the bottom and may climb the whole height, which makes O(n log n).

blocks.caption: Green subtrees are finished heaps. Watch them merge, bottom up.

blocks.code:
def build_min_heap(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):        # every parent, bottom up
        sift_down(nums, i, n)
    return nums

def sift_down(heap, i, n):
    while True:
        left, right = 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
        smallest = i
        if left < n and heap[left] < heap[smallest]:
            smallest = left
        if right < n and heap[right] < heap[smallest]:
            smallest = right
        if smallest == i:                      # both children are bigger or equal
            return
        heap[i], heap[smallest] = heap[smallest], heap[i]
        i = smallest

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** This is what Python's `heapq.heapify`, C++'s `make_heap`, Java's `PriorityQueue` constructor (given a collection) and the course's `Heap.from` all do.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. Optimal: O(n log n) time, O(1) space. Best: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: **Empty array** and **one value** — no parents at all (`⌊n/2⌋ − 1 < 0`): return it unchanged.
**Already a heap** — `[1, 2, 3, 4]`: every sift down stops at once.
**Sorted in reverse** — `[6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]`: the worst case, and still O(n) for bottom-up.
**Duplicates and negatives** — `[2, -1, 2, -1]`: use `<`, not `<=`, when choosing a child, so equal values don't swap for nothing.
**Build a max-heap** — flip both comparisons in `siftDown`: pick the **larger** child.
**Convert a Min Heap to a Max Heap** — ignore the old order and run the max-heap version: O(n).
**Is an array a heap?** — the check from *What is a heap?*: one pass over the parents, O(n).
**Heap Sort** — build a max-heap with this, then repeatedly move the top to the end. Next lesson.
